questions.q: A data team must run a containerized Python ETL job every night. They want no servers to manage and no Kubernetes. Which design has the least operational overhead?

options.t: An EKS cluster with managed node groups and a CronJob
options.why: Wrong: works, but adds a control-plane fee and Kubernetes operations.

options.t: An ECS task on Fargate triggered by EventBridge Scheduler
options.why: Right: serverless compute plus a cron/rate schedule with an ECS target; nothing to patch.

options.t: An EC2 Auto Scaling group running the container 24/7
options.why: Wrong: idle instances cost money and need patching.

options.t: A Lambda function with the container image
options.why: Wrong: Lambda is capped at 15 minutes, which a heavy ETL job may exceed.

questions.explain: Fargate plus EventBridge Scheduler is the simplest serverless nightly container job.
questions.remember: Containerized scheduled job with least ops and no K8s skills → ECS Fargate task started by EventBridge Scheduler.
variants: Needs queues, retries and array fan-out → AWS Batch.
Team already standardised on Kubernetes → EKS CronJob.
Run time under 15 minutes and event-driven → Lambda.

questions.q: An ECS Fargate task fails to start because it cannot pull its image from ECR and cannot read a Secrets Manager secret at launch. Which IAM role is missing permissions?

options.t: The task role
options.why: Wrong: the task role is used by the application code after the task has started.

options.t: The EC2 container instance role
options.why: Wrong: Fargate has no container instances.

options.t: The service-linked role of Auto Scaling
options.why: Wrong: unrelated to image pulls and secrets.

options.t: The task execution role
options.why: Right: ECS uses it to pull from ECR, send logs and fetch secrets at task start.

questions.explain: Platform actions at launch use the execution role.
questions.remember: Pull image, write logs, inject secrets at start → task execution role. App calls to S3/DynamoDB → task role.
variants: The app gets AccessDenied reading S3 → fix the task role.
ECS on EC2 pulling images → container instance role (or execution role).
EKS pods pulling images → node IAM role.

questions.q: A Secrets Manager database password was rotated, but running ECS tasks still use the old value. What is the correct fix?

options.t: Update the task role policy
options.why: Wrong: permissions are not the issue.

options.t: Wait for the ECS agent to refresh environment variables
options.why: Wrong: secrets are not refreshed while a task runs.

options.t: Force a new deployment so tasks restart and fetch the secret again
options.why: Right: secrets are injected as environment variables only at task start.

options.t: Enable ECS Exec on the service
options.why: Wrong: ECS Exec only opens a shell; it does not refresh secrets.

questions.explain: Secrets are read at task start, so tasks must be restarted.
questions.remember: ECS injects secrets at start → redeploy (force new deployment) to pick up rotated values.
variants: EKS with Secrets Store CSI driver → rotation can sync to mounted files.
Secret must never sit in the image → use the task definition secrets field.
Rotation itself → Secrets Manager.

questions.q: Fargate tasks in private subnets with no NAT gateway fail with CannotPullContainerError. Which change fixes this at the lowest cost and keeps traffic private?

options.t: Assign public IPs to the tasks
options.why: Wrong: works but exposes tasks and is not recommended for production.

options.t: Add a NAT gateway in every AZ
options.why: Wrong: works, but adds hourly and per-GB charges.

options.t: Copy the images to Docker Hub
options.why: Wrong: adds rate limits and internet dependency.

options.t: Add ECR api and dkr interface endpoints plus an S3 gateway endpoint
options.why: Right: layers are served from S3, so all three are needed for private pulls.

questions.explain: ECR needs api, dkr and S3 gateway endpoints for a private pull path.
questions.remember: Private-subnet image pulls without internet → com.amazonaws.<r>.ecr.api, ecr.dkr and an S3 gateway endpoint.
variants: Tasks also log to CloudWatch Logs → add a Logs endpoint.
Secrets fetched at start → Secrets Manager endpoint.
Heavy pulls through NAT cost per GB → endpoints are cheaper.

questions.q: A batch pipeline uses stateless ECS Fargate workers that tolerate interruption. How can cost be reduced while keeping a minimum of reliable capacity?

options.t: Use Fargate Spot only, with base 0
options.why: Wrong: all tasks could be reclaimed at once.

options.t: Use a capacity provider strategy with a base of FARGATE tasks and the rest weighted to FARGATE_SPOT
options.why: Right: base keeps guaranteed On-Demand tasks; weight shifts the remainder to cheaper Spot.

options.t: Mix an Auto Scaling group provider and Fargate Spot in one strategy
options.why: Wrong: a strategy can only use one type of provider.

options.t: Move to EKS with extended support
options.why: Wrong: extended support raises control-plane cost.

questions.explain: Base plus weight blends On-Demand reliability with Spot savings.
questions.remember: Cheap but available Fargate → capacity provider strategy: base on FARGATE, weight toward FARGATE_SPOT.
variants: Spot interruption warning → 2 minutes (SIGTERM); handle gracefully.
EC2 Spot → ASG capacity provider.
Steady 24/7 load → Compute Savings Plans.

questions.q: A Step Functions workflow must run a container step on ECS and continue only after the container finishes, failing the state if the exit code is non-zero. Which integration fits?

options.t: ecs:runTask with the default request-response pattern
options.why: Wrong: it returns immediately after starting the task.

options.t: ecs:runTask.sync
options.why: Right: runs the task and waits for completion; a non-zero exit code fails the state.

options.t: ecs:runTask.waitForTaskToken only
options.why: Wrong: needs the container to call back with a token; not required here.

options.t: An EventBridge rule with a polling Lambda
options.why: Wrong: extra moving parts for a built-in capability.

questions.explain: The .sync pattern waits for the ECS task to stop.
questions.remember: Run a container in a workflow and wait for it → Step Functions ecs:runTask.sync.
variants: Container reports back custom results → .waitForTaskToken.
Airflow instead of Step Functions → EcsRunTaskOperator in MWAA.
Run a Batch job and wait → batch:submitJob.sync.

questions.q: Thousands of queued containerized jobs need priorities, automatic retries and array-job fan-out. Which approach is best?

options.t: Plain ECS RunTask calls from a script
options.why: Wrong: RunTask has no queue, retries, priorities or array jobs.

options.t: A Kubernetes Deployment on EKS
options.why: Wrong: a Deployment is for long-running replicas, not job queues.

options.t: An ECS service with desired count 1000
options.why: Wrong: services keep tasks running; they do not schedule queued jobs.

options.t: AWS Batch on ECS/Fargate
options.why: Right: Batch adds job queues, priorities, retries and array jobs on top of ECS.

questions.explain: Batch is the scheduler layer above ECS/EKS.
questions.remember: Queues, retries, priorities, array jobs → AWS Batch, not raw RunTask.
variants: Simple retry and flow control only → Step Functions.
Just run one container → ECS RunTask.
Batch jobs on existing K8s → AWS Batch on EKS.

questions.q: New releases of an ECS service sometimes crash on start. The team wants the deployment to stop and automatically return to the last working version. What should be enabled?

options.t: A deployment circuit breaker with rollback
options.why: Right: detects tasks that never reach steady state, stops the deployment and reverts.

options.t: Task protection
options.why: Wrong: protects tasks from scale-in, not from bad deployments.

options.t: A DAEMON scheduling strategy
options.why: Wrong: places one task per EC2 instance; unrelated.

options.t: ECS Exec
options.why: Wrong: a debugging shell, not a rollback tool.

questions.explain: The circuit breaker with rollback automates recovery from failed rollouts.
questions.remember: Bad release keeps failing → ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback; turn it on for every service.
variants: Test traffic before cutover with bake time → native ECS blue/green with lifecycle hooks.
Roll back on alarms → CloudWatch alarms in the deployment config.
Older managed blue/green → CodeDeploy.

questions.q: A company already runs Spark and other apps on Kubernetes and wants AWS to manage the control plane. They also want Spark jobs on the same cluster using the EMR-optimized runtime. What should they use?

options.t: ECS on Fargate
options.why: Wrong: not Kubernetes, so existing manifests and operators do not apply.

options.t: EMR Serverless
options.why: Wrong: no cluster at all, so it does not share the existing EKS cluster.

options.t: Amazon EKS with EMR on EKS
options.why: Right: managed K8s control plane, and a virtual cluster mapped to a namespace runs Spark with EMR runtime.

options.t: Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2
options.why: Wrong: you would operate the control plane yourself.

questions.explain: EMR on EKS runs Spark jobs on an existing EKS cluster.
questions.remember: Spark on an existing Kubernetes cluster → EMR on EKS; no cluster wanted → EMR Serverless.
variants: Least ops containers, no K8s skills → ECS Fargate.
Open-source Spark operator instead of EMR runtime → possible but self-managed.
Use Karpenter and Spot for executors to cut cost.

questions.q: Pods on EKS must access an S3 bucket. The same IAM role has to be reused across ten clusters without editing its trust policy each time. Which solution fits?

options.t: IRSA with one OIDC provider per cluster
options.why: Wrong: each cluster needs its own OIDC provider and trust edits.

options.t: The node IAM role
options.why: Wrong: every pod on the node would share its permissions.

options.t: Long-term access keys in Kubernetes Secrets
options.why: Wrong: static keys are insecure and hard to rotate.

options.t: EKS Pod Identity
options.why: Right: the role trusts pods.eks.amazonaws.com, so it is reusable across clusters.

questions.explain: Pod Identity uses a single service principal in the trust policy.
questions.remember: Same role across many clusters, simple setup → EKS Pod Identity (association via the EKS API, trusts pods.eks.amazonaws.com).
variants: Pods on Fargate → IRSA, because Pod Identity is not supported there.
Windows nodes or EKS Anywhere → not supported by Pod Identity.
Limit per cluster → 5,000 associations.

questions.q: Pods running on AWS Fargate for EKS need permissions to read DynamoDB. Which approach works?

options.t: EKS Pod Identity
options.why: Wrong: not supported on Fargate.

options.t: IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA)
options.why: Right: IRSA works on Fargate through the cluster OIDC provider.

options.t: The Fargate node role shared by all pods
options.why: Wrong: there is no node you can give shared credentials to, and it violates least privilege.

options.t: An EC2 instance profile
options.why: Wrong: Fargate has no EC2 instance you manage.

questions.explain: Pod Identity is Linux EC2 only; Fargate pods use IRSA.
questions.remember: Fargate pods needing AWS access → IRSA (Pod Identity unsupported on Fargate, Windows, Outposts).
variants: Linux EC2 nodes, simpler setup → Pod Identity.
Fargate profile limits → no DaemonSets, GPUs, privileged pods.
Pod Identity credential endpoint → 169.254.170.23 (add to NO_PROXY).

questions.q: A platform team finds EKS node patching, add-on upgrades and scaling too much work but wants to stay on Kubernetes with EC2 instance choice. Which option reduces the overhead most?

options.t: Self-managed node groups
options.why: Wrong: maximum control means maximum work.

options.t: EKS Auto Mode
options.why: Right: AWS manages Karpenter-based compute, node OS patching and core add-ons, for an extra per-instance fee.

options.t: Moving to ECS Anywhere
options.why: Wrong: changes orchestrator and is for on-premises.

options.t: EKS Anywhere
options.why: Wrong: runs Kubernetes on-prem and increases the work.

questions.explain: Auto Mode is the closest to serverless Kubernetes while keeping EC2.
questions.remember: Cut EKS data-plane operations → EKS Auto Mode (extra management fee); some pods only → Fargate profiles.
variants: Avoid Kubernetes entirely → ECS Fargate.
On-prem machines as nodes of an EKS cluster → EKS Hybrid Nodes.
Managed node groups handle drain-and-replace updates but you still choose instances.

questions.q: An EKS cluster control-plane cost suddenly became six times higher. The cluster runs an old Kubernetes version. What is the likely cause and fix?

options.t: The cluster entered extended support at $0.60/h; upgrade to a standard-support version
options.why: Right: standard is $0.10/h; extended adds $0.50/h after 14 months.

options.t: Auto Mode was enabled; disable it
options.why: Wrong: Auto Mode adds a per-instance fee, not a 6x control-plane cost.

options.t: Fargate Spot interruptions; use On-Demand
options.why: Wrong: unrelated to control-plane pricing.

options.t: The ECS control plane fee changed
options.why: Wrong: ECS has no control-plane fee, and this is EKS.

questions.explain: Each version has 14 months of standard then 12 months of extended support at a higher price.
questions.remember: Unexpected EKS bill jump with an old version → extended support ($0.60/h vs $0.10/h); upgrade one minor version at a time.
variants: Many small clusters → consolidate, each costs about $73/month.
ECS control plane → free.
Very large clusters → Provisioned Control Plane tiers.

questions.q: An EKS pod is stuck with the error "failed to assign an IP address to container". Which fix addresses the root cause?

options.t: Raise the memory limit of the pod
options.why: Wrong: memory limits cause OOMKilled, not IP errors.

options.t: Add a liveness probe
options.why: Wrong: probes do not allocate IP addresses.

options.t: Enable prefix delegation, a secondary CIDR with custom networking, bigger subnets or IPv6
options.why: Right: VPC CNI gives each pod a real VPC IP, so small subnets run out.

options.t: Replace the node role
options.why: Wrong: the node role does not affect IP allocation.

questions.explain: The VPC CNI is out of IPs in the subnet.
questions.remember: EKS IP assignment failure → subnet IP exhaustion; use prefix delegation, secondary CIDR (100.64.0.0/10), larger subnets or IPv6.
variants: ECS awsvpc tasks cannot scale → bigger or more subnets (one IP per task).
Pods per node limit → ENIs × IPs per ENI.
ImagePullBackOff → node role ECR access or endpoints.

questions.q: An ECS task stops with exit code 137. What does this indicate and what should be done?

options.t: A segmentation fault; rebuild the image
options.why: Wrong: a segfault is exit code 139.

options.t: It was stopped by SIGTERM during scale-in; nothing is wrong
options.why: Wrong: that is exit code 143.

options.t: A normal application error; read logs only
options.why: Wrong: generic app errors are usually exit 1 or 2.

options.t: The container exceeded its memory hard limit (OOM); raise memory or fix the leak
options.why: Right: the container was killed when it went over the hard memory limit.

questions.explain: 137 means killed for exceeding memory (OOM).
questions.remember: Exit 137 → OOM, raise memory; 1/2 → app error (check logs); 139 → segfault; 143 → SIGTERM (scale-in, deployment, Spot).
variants: Same condition on EKS → pod OOMKilled; raise limits/requests.
Handle SIGTERM within stopTimeout.
Soft memory setting → memoryReservation.

questions.q: Builds in a pipeline fail randomly because of Docker Hub pull rate limits, and the company wants cached images kept private and scannable. Which feature fits?

options.t: ECR cross-Region replication
options.why: Wrong: replicates your own ECR images, not upstream registries.

options.t: An ECR pull-through cache rule for Docker Hub
options.why: Right: first pull fetches upstream, later pulls come from private ECR; credentials sit in Secrets Manager.

options.t: Lifecycle policies
options.why: Wrong: delete images; they do not avoid rate limits.

options.t: Tag immutability
options.why: Wrong: controls overwriting tags only.

questions.explain: Pull-through cache avoids Docker Hub limits and outages.
questions.remember: Docker Hub rate limits → ECR pull-through cache (credentials in Secrets Manager with prefix ecr-pullthroughcache/; up to 50 rules).
variants: Images close to compute in several Regions → cross-Region replication.
Cross-account pulls → repository policy plus IAM permissions.
Slow start of large images on Fargate → SOCI lazy loading.

questions.q: Security requires ECR images to be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, and another account's ECS tasks must pull them. What must be done?

options.t: Change the repository encryption to KMS after it is created
options.why: Wrong: encryption is set at repository creation and cannot be changed later.

options.t: Create the repository with KMS and a customer managed key, add a repository policy, and grant the puller key access
options.why: Right: cross-account pulls need the repository policy, IAM permissions in the pulling account, and KMS key access.

options.t: Use basic scanning on the repository
options.why: Wrong: scanning does not control encryption.

options.t: Share the registry authorization token
options.why: Wrong: tokens are temporary (12 hours) and sharing them is not an access model.

questions.explain: Encryption is chosen at creation, and cross-account pulls need policy plus key access.
questions.remember: Cross-account ECR pull with CMK → repository policy (or PrincipalOrgID) + IAM pull permissions + KMS key permissions.
variants: Default encryption → AES-256 with S3-managed keys.
Docker login token lifetime → 12 hours.
Separate CI push and runtime pull roles.

questions.q: Security wants continuous detection of crypto-mining and reverse shells inside running ECS Fargate and EKS containers. Which service feature fits?

options.t: ECR basic scanning
options.why: Wrong: scans images for OS CVEs, not runtime behaviour.

options.t: AWS Config rule ecs-containers-nonprivileged
options.why: Wrong: checks configuration, not runtime activity.

options.t: GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring
options.why: Right: an agent detects threats like crypto-mining, reverse shells and privilege escalation on ECS (incl. Fargate), EKS and EC2.

options.t: CloudTrail data events
options.why: Wrong: audit API calls; they do not see in-container behaviour.

questions.explain: Runtime Monitoring covers running containers.
questions.remember: Malicious activity inside running containers → GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring; Kubernetes audit log analysis → GuardDuty EKS Protection.
variants: Continuous CVE scan of OS and Python packages in images → ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector).
Config drift on EKS → rules like eks-secrets-encrypted.
EKS audit logs to CloudWatch → enable the audit log type.

questions.q: A team needs a simple web API running from a container image with an ALB, URL and auto scaling in minutes, and AWS App Runner is no longer available to new customers. What should they choose?

options.t: ECS Express Mode
options.why: Right: deploys a web app from just an image and sets up ALB, URL, networking and scaling at no extra charge.

options.t: EKS Auto Mode
options.why: Wrong: far more setup and a per-cluster fee.

options.t: ECS Anywhere
options.why: Wrong: is for on-premises servers.

options.t: AWS Batch
options.why: Wrong: is for batch jobs, not web APIs.

questions.explain: Express Mode is the replacement path for App Runner.
questions.remember: Fastest managed web app from an image → ECS Express Mode (up to 25 services share one ALB).
variants: On-prem servers managed from ECS → ECS Anywhere.
Existing Kubernetes → EKS.
GPU inference without managing AMIs → ECS Managed Instances.

questions.q: A team needs per-task CPU and memory dashboards for ECS and per-pod metrics for EKS, plus PromQL dashboards for EKS. Which pairing is correct?

options.t: CloudWatch Container Insights for utilization; Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus with Managed Grafana for PromQL
options.why: Right: Container Insights covers cluster/task/pod metrics; AMP plus Grafana gives PromQL on EKS.

options.t: AWS Config for utilization; X-Ray for PromQL
options.why: Wrong: Config tracks configuration and X-Ray traces requests.

options.t: CloudTrail for utilization; Athena for PromQL
options.why: Wrong: CloudTrail logs API calls.

options.t: ECR enhanced scanning for utilization; Inspector for PromQL
options.why: Wrong: those are security scans.

questions.explain: Container Insights plus Managed Prometheus and Grafana is the standard stack.
questions.remember: Container utilization metrics → Container Insights; PromQL and Grafana on EKS → Managed Service for Prometheus + Managed Grafana; tracing → ADOT with X-Ray.
variants: Alert on ECS task state changes → ECS events to EventBridge.
Container logs to S3 or Firehose → FireLens (Fluent Bit).
EKS control plane logs → enable each log type; audit for security.
